A001.plainWords: Eudaimonia isn't a good mood or a nice weekend. Aristotle means a whole life lived well, over decades. So when you're choosing, don't only ask what feels good now. Ask what kind of person, and what kind of life, this choice makes more possible.
A001.example: Taking the job with the better title but a commute that eats your evenings with your kids: the real question is what that trade does to the life you're building.

A002.plainWords: Aristotle's thought is that a thing is good when it does what it's distinctively for. A knife cuts well. People, he says, reason and act on that reasoning. So flourishing isn't an add-on to life, it's doing that human work well. What's yours?
A002.example: A nurse who's skilled at the paperwork but gets her energy from sitting with frightened patients might ask whether her best work is the part nobody tracks.

A003.plainWords: Rules tell you what to do in a given moment. Virtue is a settled habit of choosing well, so you don't have to look it up. Aristotle says to put your effort there. Results come and go; character is the thing that produces them.
A003.example: Someone who is honest because it's who they are doesn't agonise over whether to admit the billing error. They just call and fix it.

A004.plainWords: Reading about courage won't make you courageous. You get there by doing brave things, badly at first. Aristotle puts the order plainly: act first, and the disposition builds. Waiting until you feel brave or feel like a generous person is waiting for the wrong thing.
A004.example: You become someone who speaks up in meetings by speaking up once, shakily, in a small one, not by rehearsing confidence in the mirror.

A005.plainWords: Too much and too little both miss. Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and waste. But the middle isn't an average you can calculate. It shifts with the situation, the person, and the point. The target is whatever fits.
A005.example: Being honest with a grieving friend doesn't mean listing every flaw in the eulogy. It also doesn't mean saying nothing. The right amount depends on who's in the room.

A006.plainWords: Aristotle doesn't pretend virtue is enough. A person with no money, no friends, and no security isn't going to flourish just by being good. Some outside things are real conditions. So caring about justice and decent material conditions is part of the job, not a distraction from it.
A006.example: A talented kid who skips meals and works nights to help their family isn't failing at character. The conditions are doing the damage, and fixing them counts as ethical work.

A007.plainWords: Desire isn't the enemy and reason isn't a jailer. Aristotle wants them working together, with appetite trained over time to want what's good for you. Crushing desire leaves it stronger underground. Teaching it, through habit and practice, works better.
A007.example: A person who has lived on a budget long enough stops feeling the pull toward the expensive coffee. Years of small choices changed the wanting itself.

A008.plainWords: One good day doesn't make you flourishing, and one bad year doesn't end it. Aristotle says to judge the whole arc. That means you shouldn't collapse at a setback or relax at a win. Ask which way your life is heading overall.
A008.example: Losing a job in your forties is a hard chapter, but if the last ten years built skills, friends, and habits, it isn't the verdict on your life.

A009.plainWords: Doing the right thing is the start. Aristotle's ideal person also does it well, with grace and proportion, so the act looks like what it is. Ethics and beauty aren't separate departments. A kindness done grudgingly or clumsily loses something.
A009.example: Returning a lost wallet is good. Doing it warmly, without a lecture or a reward-hint, is the version people remember.

A010.plainWords: A good life can be wrecked by terrible luck, and Aristotle says so. What virtue gives you is resilience, not armour. You recover better, and you respond more wisely. So don't expect to be untouchable. Expect to be able to cope with what lands.
A010.example: A well-run family business burns in a fire. The owners who have honest relationships and savings rebuild faster than those who only had the building.

A011.plainWords: Courage isn't having no fear. Aristotle puts it between cowardice and recklessness: you act well in the face of what's truly frightening, for something worth it. Pick the fear that's worth facing, and start small enough that you can actually do it.
A011.example: Someone afraid of public speaking who volunteers for a two-minute update at a team meeting is practising courage, far more than the person who jumps off a cliff for a dare.

A012.plainWords: Temperance isn't giving up pleasure. Aristotle means enjoying it well: the right amount, at the right time, in the right way. The point is that you train your appetites instead of letting them train you. Someone who can enjoy dinner without it running the evening has it.
A012.example: Having two squares of dark chocolate and actually tasting them, rather than finishing the bar while scrolling, is a small piece of temperance.

A013.plainWords: Giving well means the right amount to the right people at the right time, for the right reasons. Aristotle says it should cost you something but not ruin you. Giving too little is hoarding. Giving everything isn't virtue, it's another kind of poor judgement.
A013.example: Donating a steady slice of your income to a cause you've checked is generosity. Handing over your rent to every sad story on social media is something else.

A014.plainWords: Magnificence is generosity at a large scale: spending big on something public that lasts. Aristotle says the test isn't the number, it's whether the spending fits and serves others, not your image. If you have resources, ask what they could build for more than just you.
A014.example: A successful baker who pays for a community oven in the local park is doing it. A name on a stadium for ego's sake isn't.

A015.plainWords: The magnanimous person knows they're capable of great things and is right about it. They're not flattened by bad luck or puffed up by good luck. So the aim is an honest sense of your own worth, neither too big nor too small.
A015.example: A designer who knows she's good enough to apply for the top studio, and who doesn't fall apart when she's rejected, has a steady sense of her worth.

A016.plainWords: Honour matters to the person of good character, but it isn't the top goal. Seek recognition for the right things, in proportion. Don't chase it for itself, and don't pretend you don't want it when you've earned it.
A016.example: Accepting a promotion you worked for, with thanks and without false modesty, is proper ambition. Angling for a title just to be seen with it isn't.

A017.plainWords: Anger isn't something to remove. Aristotle wants it proportioned: at the right things, with the right people, in the right way, for the right length of time. Someone who never gets angry at anything is missing something. So is someone who stays furious for a week.
A017.example: Raising your voice once when a contractor ignores a safety rule is gentleness in his sense. Sulking for days over a late reply isn't.

A018.plainWords: Between always agreeing and always arguing there's a middle: being pleasant in the right way, with the right people, at the right moment. Not everyone gets the same warmth, but nobody gets contempt. It's a skill of reading the room without losing yourself.
A018.example: A colleague who says "I see it differently, can I show you why?" is friendly. The one who nods at everything and the one who contradicts everything both aren't.

A019.plainWords: Truthfulness about yourself means claiming what's accurate, no more and no less. Boasting is one way to miss. Running yourself down is another. Aristotle treats this as calibration, not confession: you're telling people the actual size of the thing.
A019.example: Describing your role as "I ran the project" if you did, and "I helped with the budget" if that was your part, is truthfulness. Inflating or shrinking either one isn't.

A020.plainWords: Between the boor who can't joke and the clown who can't stop, there's wit. Aristotle thinks good humour is a virtue: it eases tension and shows perspective. You're serious about the right things and light about the rest. Don't take yourself so seriously that laughing becomes impossible.
A020.example: Laughing at your own burnt dinner in front of guests puts everyone at ease. Joking about a guest's divorce doesn't.

A021.plainWords: Shame in Aristotle's sense is the felt sense of what would disgrace you, closer to reputation than to guilt. It's a brake. A person who feels no shame at anything has lost it. So know what would disgrace you, and let that guide you without crushing you.
A021.example: Feeling a flush of embarrassment before you pad an expense report is useful. It's the brake working, and you can listen to it.

A022.plainWords: Righteous indignation sits between envy, which hurts at another's good luck, and spite, which enjoys another's bad luck. It's pain at undeserved fortune and pleasure at deserved. Think of it as justice felt in the body. Feel it when the wrong people get honoured and the right ones are overlooked.
A022.example: Being angry that a colleague who took credit got the promotion, while your quieter teammate who did the work got nothing, is indignation. Resenting the teammate's raise is envy.

A023.plainWords: Justice, for Aristotle, is virtue as it shows up with other people. It has two faces: handing out goods in proportion, and putting things right after a wrong. In daily dealings, ask what's fair, what's owed, and whether the thing is proportionate.
A023.example: Splitting a group project's credit by who did what, and offering to redo a section you botched, covers both sides of it.

A024.plainWords: Beyond giving, there's using what you have well. The liberal person knows what to spend, save, give away, and refuse. Aristotle asks you to treat your money and things as a skill to practise, not a pile to build.
A024.example: Someone who puts aside a year of savings, funds a nephew's course, and says no to a flashy car has a settled sense of what money is for.

A025.plainWords: Proper pride is knowing you're worthy of great things and saying so truthfully. Aristotle puts it between vanity and false humility. Playing small isn't a virtue, it's failing to acknowledge what you've actually earned.
A025.example: Telling an interviewer "I rebuilt that system from scratch" when you did is proper pride. Mumbling "oh, I just helped a bit" isn't.

A026.plainWords: Not every slight deserves a reply. The patient person lets small wrongs pass and saves effort for what matters. The skill is sorting. Some things must be addressed, some should be let go, and the difference is a judgement you make each time.
A026.example: A neighbour's bin left out for two days isn't worth a note. A neighbour's dog attacking yours is.

A027.plainWords: Good fortune tests you as much as bad. Aristotle says the person unchanged by success, neither arrogant nor complacent, has passed the harder test. When things go well, keep the habits that got you there.
A027.example: A team that wins a big contract and keeps the same careful weekly review is doing it. A team that stops after the win usually doesn't win the next.

A028.plainWords: Hard times don't build character, they show it. Aristotle's resilient person draws on what they built when things were easier. So build your character when it's cheap, and it holds when it's expensive.
A028.example: Someone who has spent years keeping promises in small things is more likely to keep one when keeping it costs them dearly.

A029.plainWords: Anger isn't always wrong. Someone who never gets angry at injustice is deficient, not saintly. Aristotle asks whether it's the right size, aimed at the right target, and expressed the right way. So don't suppress it. Train it.
A029.example: Being furious that a landlord ignored mould in a child's room, and writing a firm letter, is anger well used. Shouting at the child about it isn't.

A030.plainWords: Integrity is the virtues working together in what you do. You don't say one thing and do another. That consistency is what makes someone reliable. Others can predict you, and so can you.
A030.example: A manager who criticises long hours and then sends emails at midnight is giving mixed signals. One who logs off on time is saying and doing the same thing.

A031.plainWords: Synesis is the knack of judging well in practical matters: seeing what follows from what, and catching when a conclusion doesn't follow. It's a skill. You build it by following arguments all the way to the end, instead of stopping where it feels comfortable.
A031.example: Hearing "we've always done it this way, so it works" and asking what actually follows from that is the skill. Nodding along isn't.

A032.plainWords: Euboulia is deliberating well: reaching a good decision in a good way, in good time. It isn't cleverness. It's the practical ability to think through what to do. Over-thinking and snap judgements both miss it.
A032.example: Spending an evening listing options and consequences before choosing a flat, rather than signing in ten minutes or dithering for a month, is it.

A033.plainWords: Some truths you can't prove from anything earlier. You just see them, and everything else gets built on top. Aristotle calls that grasp nous. Trust your intuitions enough to take them seriously, then check them against what actually happens.
A033.example: A carpenter feels a joint is wrong before she can say why. She trusts the feeling, tests it with a clamp, and finds it was right.

A034.plainWords: Knowing that something is true is one thing. Knowing why is another. Aristotle prizes the second: understanding causes, not just collecting facts. Wanting to understand is a habit, and it changes how you read and what you ask.
A034.example: Memorising that interest compounds is knowing. Working out on paper why a small difference in rate gives such a big gap after thirty years is understanding.

A035.plainWords: Making things well takes more than a knack. Aristotle's techne means you understand why the method works. So make something with your hands and your head. What a maker knows can't be borrowed from anyone who hasn't made it.
A035.example: Baking the same loaf ten times and changing one thing each time teaches you more about bread than reading ten recipes.

A036.plainWords: Sophia is the top of Aristotle's intellectual ladder: grasping first principles and the reasoning built on them, about the biggest questions. It needs room. So set aside real time, uninterrupted, for the large questions you normally brush off.
A036.example: A long walk with no podcast, thinking about what the point of your work is, counts. So does an afternoon with one hard book.

A037.plainWords: Cleverness finds a way to get whatever you're after, good or bad. Practical wisdom is cleverness aimed at something worth getting. Aristotle doesn't mind being clever. He minds smart people serving poor goals. Check what yours is for.
A037.example: A brilliant marketer who builds a sleek campaign to sell people things they don't need is clever. Using the same skill to get a useful product noticed is wise.

A038.plainWords: Gnome is judging a particular case fairly, especially when the rules don't quite fit. It goes past "what follows from what" to "what's decent here?" You build it by weighing real situations, one at a time, and asking what fairness asks.
A038.example: A teacher gives an extension to a student whose parent was in hospital, though the policy says no. She can explain why it's fair to the rest of the class.

A039.plainWords: In practice, the person who's done it often beats the person who's read about it. They may not be able to state the rules, but they get the case right. So don't dismiss people just because they lack the vocabulary or the degree.
A039.example: A veteran bus driver knows which stop gets rowdy on Fridays and how to prevent it. No manual says so.

A040.plainWords: Virtues aren't separate gadgets. They're one character. Courage without temperance turns reckless. Generosity without justice turns arbitrary. So don't polish one trait and ignore the rest. Work on the whole person.
A040.example: Someone proud of being brave who ignores fairness will cheerfully charge in to rescue one friend while shortchanging everyone else.

A041.plainWords: The good person acts for what's noble, not just what's useful or pleasant. Aristotle calls that kalon: the fine, the beautiful. Taste and ethics overlap. So ask not only "does it work?" but "is it worth being the kind of person who does this?"
A041.example: Staying to help a stranger carry shopping up the stairs, when it earns you nothing, is the thing done for its own fineness.

A042.plainWords: Virtue is a settled disposition, not a mood. Being generous once, on a good day, doesn't make you generous. Being generous even when it's inconvenient does. So build dispositions through repetition, instead of chasing the feeling.
A042.example: Tipping well only when you're in a good mood isn't generosity. Doing it as a standing habit is.

A043.plainWords: Phronesis is knowing what this situation, with these people, actually calls for. It's no textbook, but it can be trained: through experience, reflection, and watching people who do it well. Pay attention to how good judges handle the details.
A043.example: A senior doctor who tells a patient the truth gently, at the right pace, isn't following a script. She's reading the person.

A044.plainWords: You can't learn practical judgement from a book. It comes from lived cases, paid attention to and thought about. That's why the young can be clever but not wise. They haven't seen enough. Treat your experience as your best teacher.
A044.example: Someone who has run three failed projects often sees the fourth go wrong at the planning stage. The first-time manager can't.

A045.plainWords: Deliberation isn't endless analysis. It's working out what's in your power and which path leads somewhere good, in the right order and in reasonable time, and then concluding. Don't weigh things you can't change.
A045.example: Deciding how to respond to a delayed flight means looking at rebooking options, not rehearsing why the airline failed.

A046.plainWords: Rules help, but they stop short of the real case. The wise person sees what's called for here, now, with these people. That perception is trained. So practise noticing the concrete details, not just applying the general principle.
A046.example: Telling a nervous new hire "great work" might be right. Noticing she needs a specific, honest correction instead is the trained eye at work.

A047.plainWords: The moral virtues aren't a checklist. Practical wisdom ties them into a single character. Courage without temperance isn't really courage, and generosity without justice isn't really generosity. Work on how they fit together.
A047.example: Giving a big gift while underpaying your staff doesn't add up to generosity. Wisdom spots the contradiction.

A048.plainWords: Aristotle's formula sounds simple: right way, right time, right objects, right manner. The difficulty is knowing what "right" means each time. Don't flatten it into a slogan. Let it make you look harder at the context.
A048.example: Saying "I'm sorry" sincerely and promptly after hurting someone is right. Saying it weeks later by text may not be.

A049.plainWords: When you're stuck, ask someone whose judgement you trust. Practical wisdom is partly social: wise people recognise each other and learn from each other. Test your own reasoning against the reasoning of people whose lives you admire.
A049.example: Before taking a risky job, you talk it through with a friend who has changed careers twice and is honest with you about it.

A050.plainWords: Wise action starts with seeing what matters in a situation. Aristotle says that perceptiveness can be trained. So practise noticing what others miss. The wise person often sees what's needed before they can say why.
A050.example: A host who notices the quiet guest hasn't been included, and gently draws her in, is seeing what's called for.

A051.plainWords: Applying a rule strictly can sometimes create injustice. Aristotle's equity means knowing when to bend it, for the sake of justice itself. Don't let being consistent turn into being cruel.
A051.example: A landlord who waives a late fee for a tenant who just lost a family member isn't being inconsistent. He's serving what the rule was for.

A052.plainWords: Rules are useful but not enough. The wise person knows when to follow one strictly and when to adapt it. The test is whether following it still serves the purpose it was made for.
A052.example: A "no phones at dinner" rule is great, until your daughter is waiting for news from a hospital. You make an exception, and everyone understands why.

A053.plainWords: An action is voluntary when you know what you're doing, choose it, and it starts in you. Aristotle says virtue and vice are voluntary in this sense. You're the origin of your character. So own what you do as yours.
A053.example: Telling yourself "I had no choice" about a snappy reply you sent knowingly, at your desk, with time to think, isn't quite true.

A054.plainWords: Choice isn't impulse or opinion. It's reasoned desire for something you can actually do, the point where thinking and wanting produce action. Your choices make you who you are, so don't treat them lightly.
A054.example: Choosing to apologise first, after thinking it through, is different from blurting it out or wishing you could. It shapes you.

A055.plainWords: You didn't choose where you started. You did choose the acts that shaped you. Someone became unjust by doing unjust things. That's a burden and also a freedom: you're writing who you're becoming.
A055.example: A person raised in a cynical household who starts keeping small promises as an adult is rewriting their own character, one act at a time.

A056.plainWords: Akrasia is knowing what's good and doing the other thing anyway. It's not ignorance, it's desire beating reason in the moment. Name it when it happens. Don't wave it away. It's real and almost everyone has been there.
A056.example: You know you should leave the party at midnight for tomorrow's early start. You stay until two, knowing it, and feel worse for it.

A057.plainWords: The gap between knowing and doing isn't permanent. Habit, practice, and growing wisdom gradually narrow it. Aristotle sees it as a stage of development, not a built-in flaw. So don't read your slips as final.
A057.example: A new runner who skips training days gets more reliable after a season of showing up, even without any new motivation.

A058.plainWords: The continent person feels the pull and masters it. The virtuous person doesn't feel the same pull, because desire has been trained. Self-control is a real achievement. But Aristotle says aim past it, toward a character where doing well feels natural.
A058.example: Resisting the biscuit tin through willpower is continence. Not wanting it by mid-afternoon, because your meals now keep you full, is something more.

A059.plainWords: A person with weak will knows the good and fails at it. A vicious person doesn't know the good or doesn't care. Weak will can be cured. Vice is far harder. So don't confuse a lapse with a rotten character.
A059.example: A person who lies once under pressure and feels awful is in a different place than someone who lies routinely and feels nothing.

A060.plainWords: Aristotle holds you responsible for your character, but he also sees acts done in ignorance or under compulsion. Voluntary wrongs call for correction. Involuntary ones call for understanding. Be accountable without beating yourself up.
A060.example: Forgetting a friend's birthday because of a hospital stay is different from deliberately ignoring it. One needs an apology and understanding, the other needs a change.

A061.plainWords: Both kinds of act are done through ignorance. But in the involuntary case you feel regret when you find out. In the non-voluntary case you don't. Aristotle's point is that regret shows you understood the wrong.
A061.example: Someone who accidentally shares a private message and feels sick about it differs from someone who shrugs. The sick feeling is evidence of care.

A062.plainWords: Choices aren't isolated. Each one strengthens or weakens a disposition, and over time the pattern becomes character. So treat each choice as a building block, not a one-off.
A062.example: Skipping your usual walk "just once" a few times in a row quietly changes you into someone who doesn't walk.

A063.plainWords: Nobody would choose to live without friends, even with every other good thing. Aristotle says friendship is where virtue gets practised and tested. Invest in friends as part of your own flourishing, not as an extra.
A063.example: A person with a good job and a nice flat who hasn't had a real conversation in weeks is missing something no promotion supplies.

A064.plainWords: Some friendships run on usefulness, some on fun, and some on admiring each other's character and wanting the other's good. The first two are fragile. The third lasts. Know which kind you're in, and where you can, aim for the third.
A064.example: A colleague you only talk to about work and a friend you'd drive across the country for are not the same type of friend.

A065.plainWords: A true friend wants your good for your sake, not for what they get from you. Aristotle makes that the test. Ask yourself in a friendship: do I want their good, or what they give me?
A065.example: Being genuinely glad when a friend gets a job in another city, even though you'll see less of them, is the test passed.

A066.plainWords: Friendship starts with how you treat yourself. Aristotle says the good person is at peace with themselves and enjoys their own company. A person at war with themselves finds it hard to befriend anyone. Work on that first.
A066.example: Someone who can spend an evening alone without restlessness or self-criticism is usually easier company for others.

A067.plainWords: Real friendship needs a kind of equality, not in status or money but in goodwill and in giving and receiving. Unequal friendships, like parent and child, can work if the affection fits the distance. Look for mutuality in your closest ones.
A067.example: A friendship where one person always listens and the other always talks has drifted from the real thing, whatever the title says.

A068.plainWords: Good times show who's around. Bad times show who's a friend. Aristotle says the one who stays when things go wrong matters most. Be that person. Don't drop people when they become costly or awkward.
A068.example: Visiting a friend who has had a divorce and doesn't want to talk, and just sitting with her, is the test.

A069.plainWords: Concord is shared vision about what matters and how to live, not agreement on everything. In families, teams and communities, make the shared values explicit and work toward them together.
A069.example: A team that disagrees about tactics but all want customers to be well served has concord. One with no shared aim just has meetings.

A070.plainWords: The giver tends to care more about the receiver than the reverse, because they've put something of themselves in. Aristotle notes it. So don't keep a ledger of what you've given. Give freely and let it go.
A070.example: A parent who drove their kid to training for years doesn't hold it as a debt. If they start listing it, the giving has gone sour.

A071.plainWords: There are two kinds of self-love. The low kind chases honours and pleasures for yourself. The higher kind wants nobility and virtue for yourself. Aristotle says the higher one is the root of friendship and virtue.
A071.example: Wanting to be someone people can trust, even when it costs you a deal, is the higher kind. Wanting the deal at any price is the lower.

A072.plainWords: Friendship isn't only affection. It's a shared life: eating, talking, working together. The deepest kind becomes a way of living. So put time into doing things together, not just feeling warmly about each other.
A072.example: Friends who cook together every Sunday, even badly, build more than friends who text "we should catch up" for years.

A073.plainWords: Working, trading and cooperating with someone doesn't make them your friend. Friendship needs goodwill, shared values, and wishing the other well. Don't mistake useful cooperation for it, and don't ask it to carry what it can't.
A073.example: A great colleague who disappears once the project ends was a partner, not a friend. That's fine, as long as you didn't expect more.

A074.plainWords: A good friend assumes the best about your motives. Don't take offence quickly, and don't see malice where ignorance or tiredness would explain it. Reading a friend generously is itself part of friendship.
A074.example: A friend who cancels twice might be exhausted, not careless. A message asking "you okay?" does more than a cold reply.

A075.plainWords: Friendships of use end when the use ends. Friendships of pleasure end when the fun changes. Even deep ones can end if one person changes. Accept that some are seasonal, and hold the durable ones more dearly.
A075.example: Two parents who became close while their kids were in the same class often drift apart after the school years. That's a season ending, not a failure.

A076.plainWords: Friendships can span rank and ability, but they need adaptation. A parent and child, a teacher and student, an elder and a younger person, each have their own form. Don't demand sameness. Adjust to the gap.
A076.example: A grandmother and teenager who bond over cooking get along because each lets the other be what they are.

A077.plainWords: Being a friend in hard times is easy to admire. Being one in good times is harder: not envying their success, not being too busy, not taking them for granted. Celebrate your friends' luck as if it were your own.
A077.example: Showing up to a friend's launch party, and meaning your congratulations, is harder than showing up to their bad day.

A078.plainWords: A friendship that lasts needs two good people. Only someone with decent character can wish you well for your own sake and stay steady through changing fortune. So if you want good friends, start by becoming someone worth being friends with.
A078.example: You notice the friends who stayed through your messy year were the ones who were also straight with others. Like attracts like.

A079.plainWords: Pleasure isn't the good, but it isn't the enemy either. Aristotle says it's like a bloom on an activity done well. So the question isn't whether to enjoy things, it's which activities are worth enjoying.
A079.example: Enjoying a long meal with people you like, after a day of work you're proud of, belongs to a good life. Pleasure doesn't need an apology.

A080.plainWords: The best activities are chosen for their own sake, not for what they produce. The pleasure in them isn't a separate prize. It's the activity finished well. So lean toward things worth doing for themselves.
A080.example: Playing the piano badly on Sunday evening, just because you like it, counts. So does a walk with no step-tracker.

A081.plainWords: Pleasure isn't an extra ingredient you add. It's what naturally comes when you do something well. So don't hunt for pleasure directly. Do the thing, and let it arrive.
A081.example: Fixing a bike properly gives a quiet satisfaction that scrolling for it never does.

A082.plainWords: Two people can enjoy the same thing, but the pleasure differs. The good person's pleasure completes something worthwhile. The bad person's completes something low. So notice what your pleasures are finishing.
A082.example: Enjoying a competition with a rival you respect is not the same as enjoying their failure, though both feel like "winning."

A083.plainWords: Eating, drinking and sex are necessary, not the top of the ladder. Aristotle ranks the pleasures of understanding, contemplation and friendship higher. Include the bodily ones, just don't build your life around them.
A083.example: A holiday planned entirely around meals can be lovely. A life planned that way gets thin.

A084.plainWords: Pleasure walks beside the good life as a companion, not the boss. Aristotle says to let it follow virtue, not lead it. When pleasure leads, you get dragged. When it follows, you enjoy the good life you're building.
A084.example: Enjoying the evening after finishing something hard feels different from enjoying an evening to avoid it.

A085.plainWords: Chasing pleasure too hard wears out the capacity to feel it. Novelty-seekers get numb. People who indulge every appetite lose the taste for simple things. Some restraint keeps your enjoyment alive.
A085.example: Someone who eats rich food every night finds ordinary soup bland. After a week of simple meals, it tastes good again.

A086.plainWords: Some pain is the price of growing. If you dodge all of it, you can't be brave, patient, or achieve much. Aristotle's advice: tell necessary pain from pointless suffering, and accept the necessary kind.
A086.example: Sore muscles after a first week of training are the price of getting fitter. A badly fitting shoe that rubs a blister isn't.

A087.plainWords: The pleasure of thinking lasts longer and stays satisfying longer than bodily pleasures. It's more self-sufficient and doesn't cloy. So build the capacity for it: read, think, wonder, discuss.
A087.example: Spending a Sunday on a hard book and a long chat about it can leave you more content than a day out spent buying things.

A088.plainWords: Each activity has its own pleasure. Eating, thinking and friendship feel different, and each is a different quality. Don't measure them all on one scale. Respect what is distinctive about each good activity.
A088.example: The satisfaction of solving a puzzle isn't comparable to the warmth of a long dinner, and neither needs to be ranked against the other.

A089.plainWords: Contemplation is the highest human activity for Aristotle: using the best part of you on the highest things, for its own sake. It makes nothing. So make room for it: reflection, study, wonder, simply paying attention to what is.
A089.example: Sitting with a hard question on a bench for an hour, with no phone and no goal, is contemplation in his sense.

A090.plainWords: Aristotle puts contemplation highest but doesn't say it's the only good life. The life of action, in public affairs and practical work, is also virtuous. So don't feel inadequate if you're not a thinker. Find your way and live it well.
A090.example: A person who runs a local clinic may never read philosophy and still lives a full life of virtue.

A091.plainWords: The best life mixes both. Contemplation without action goes nowhere, and action without contemplation is blind. So alternate: study the world, then act in it, then reflect on what happened.
A091.example: A teacher who tries a new method, then sits with the results over the weekend, and tweaks it, is combining the two.

A092.plainWords: Using your mind is naturally pleasant. Aristotle treats learning as part of flourishing, not a chore. Curiosity is a basic drive. Follow it, and don't let it be buried under obligations.
A092.example: A person who spends an evening reading about birdsong, for no reason, is doing something very human.

A093.plainWords: A pleasure is good when it completes something worth doing, and bad when it completes something base. The same pleasure can be fine for one person and not for another, depending on what it's attached to. Check what yours is finishing.
A093.example: Laughing with friends after a hard rehearsal is fine. Laughing at someone's expense to feel big isn't.

A094.plainWords: Aristotle calls intellect the divine part of us. Using it is how we share in the divine. You don't need religion for that. It's recognising that our capacity for truth and understanding is the best thing in us.
A094.example: The moment you finally understand a hard proof, or why a piece of music works, you feel something larger than yourself.

A095.plainWords: A life of thought needs fewer outside goods than any other. If you can find satisfaction in thinking, wonder and attention, you're less at the mercy of circumstances. Aristotle means freedom, not withdrawal.
A095.example: Someone who can be content with a book and a walk is less rattled by a missed holiday or a smaller pay rise.

A096.plainWords: Distributive justice means sharing honour, money and goods in proportion to merit. In any group you lead or belong to, ask whether rewards match contribution and need. Inequality isn't automatically unjust. Disproportion is.
A096.example: A manager who gives the biggest bonus to the person who carried the project, and explains why, is distributing fairly.

A097.plainWords: When you do wrong, put it right. When you're wronged, look for proportionate repair, not vengeance. Aristotle's corrective justice restores balance instead of adding more harm.
A097.example: Paying for the window your ball broke and offering to help fix it is corrective justice. So is a firm but fair boundary after someone wrongs you.

A098.plainWords: Some things are just by nature, the same everywhere. Others only by convention, and vary. Some acts are wrong whatever a law says. Learn to tell what's merely legal from what's actually just.
A098.example: A company may legally pay a worker nothing for an hour of required setup. Many would still call that unjust.

A099.plainWords: Political justice is the framework of laws and customs that shape a community. Part natural, part conventional. Aristotle says politics isn't separate from ethics. Some of the conditions for flourishing are political.
A099.example: A neighbourhood with good public transport makes it easier for everyone to live well, whatever their personal virtue.

A100.plainWords: Reciprocity governs exchange: give what's due, return what's received, keep it proportionate. It's not just tit-for-tat. It's fairness in giving back.
A100.example: Bringing a meal to the neighbour who helped you move isn't a tit-for-tat. It's matching their care in a fitting way.

A101.plainWords: Laws teach virtue by making you act justly before you fully understand why. Good laws help make good people. Respect them as teachers of character. Where they're unjust, work to change them instead of simply breaking them.
A101.example: Following a seat-belt law until it becomes a habit turns a rule into your own care.

A102.plainWords: Justice is proportionate, public and aims to restore. Revenge is excessive, private and aims to make someone suffer. When wronged, look for justice. The difference lies in motive, measure and method.
A102.example: Reporting a theft to the police and asking for the item back is justice. Slashing the thief's tyres isn't.

A103.plainWords: Aristotle says some acts are wrong whatever the circumstances, like murder and theft. They aren't wrong by being too much or too little. Know your own non-negotiables, and decide them before you're under pressure.
A103.example: A person who decides in advance "I'll never falsify a record" doesn't weigh it up when a boss leans on them.

A104.plainWords: Equity corrects the stiffness of law. Sometimes applying a rule rigidly causes injustice because nobody foresaw this case. The equitable person knows when to bend it for justice's sake.
A104.example: A school dropping a penalty for a student who missed an exam during a family emergency is being equitable.

A105.plainWords: Law is general and cases are specific, so no law covers everything. The gap between law and justice is filled by practical wisdom, which knows when to follow the law and when to depart from it.
A105.example: A speed limit is sensible, but a driver rushing a bleeding passenger to hospital is a case the rule didn't have in mind.

A106.plainWords: Virtue isn't inborn. It's grown through education and habit. So treat education as shaping character, not just handing over information. Support teaching that builds good people, not only skilled ones.
A106.example: A teacher who makes students practise fair debate, taking turns and admitting errors, is teaching more than the topic.

A107.plainWords: The city exists for the good life, and that needs good citizens. Education is how it makes them. Aristotle asks us to support schooling that builds virtue, not merely skills.
A107.example: A parent-teacher group that argues for time on cooperation and honesty, not just exam results, is acting on this.

A108.plainWords: Character comes through repetition. You become just by doing just things, brave by doing brave things. Early attempts are awkward and deliberate, later ones become natural. Don't wait for the mood.
A108.example: A person trying to be more patient starts by pausing before every reply for a week. By week four it happens without effort.

A109.plainWords: Aristotle says moral education has to begin young, when the soul is most formable. Childhood habits shape the adult. If you have children, take it seriously. If you're educating yourself, start from where you are.
A109.example: Teaching a five-year-old to say thank you and mean it is an early lesson. You can start at forty with one small habit.

A110.plainWords: Music and the arts aren't just entertainment. They shape what you enjoy and dislike. Aristotle recommends art that lifts: music, poetry and drama that teach you to feel the right things.
A110.example: A play that makes you feel real sympathy for someone you'd normally dismiss trains something in you.

A111.plainWords: We work in order to have leisure, not the other way round. Leisure isn't idleness. It's free activity for its own sake: thinking, friendship, play. Don't mistake it for consumption.
A111.example: Spending Saturday cooking with friends and talking is leisure. Spending it clicking through shopping apps is something else.

A112.plainWords: Amusement is a rest from work, not a goal. Leisure is higher: activity for its own sake. Aristotle says to arrange life around leisure, not just amusement.
A112.example: Binge-watching to recover from work is amusement. Spending the same hours learning the guitar is closer to leisure.

A113.plainWords: Ethics begins at home. Relationships between parents and children, partners, and others in the household are where most virtue is practised. Treat your household as your main school of character.
A113.example: How you handle a spilled drink at dinner teaches more about patience than any lecture.

A114.plainWords: Emotions aren't just raw feelings. They carry judgements. Anger judges injustice, fear judges danger, pity judges undeserved suffering. So read your emotions as judgements you can examine.
A114.example: Feeling furious at a colleague contains a judgement that you were treated unfairly. You can ask whether that's true.

A115.plainWords: Aristotle defines anger as distress wanting visible revenge after a visible slight. It contains a judgement: that you've been wronged and revenge fits. So check both. Was the slight real, and is revenge appropriate?
A115.example: Someone didn't thank you in a meeting. You feel angry. Asking "was that a slight, or just forgetfulness?" changes what you do next.

A116.plainWords: Fear is distress about imagined future harm. It judges that something bad is coming and that you're vulnerable. So check the picture. Is the harm real? Are you as exposed as it feels?
A116.example: Dreading a talk, you picture the room laughing. Asking what's most likely to happen puts the fear in proportion.

A117.plainWords: Pity is pain at suffering that looks undeserved and could happen to you or yours. It judges the suffering as undeserved and yourself as vulnerable. Use it where it's warranted, but check whether the suffering really is undeserved.
A117.example: Feeling for a laid-off colleague is warranted. Asking whether it was truly out of their control keeps your pity honest.

A118.plainWords: Shame is distress about things that would bring disrepute. It judges that what you did would diminish you in others' eyes. Healthy shame guides behaviour. Toxic shame attacks the person. Learn to tell them apart.
A118.example: Feeling uneasy about padding an expense claim is healthy. Replaying an awkward comment from years ago and feeling worthless isn't.

A119.plainWords: Envy is pain at someone else's good fortune, and it judges that their success shrinks you. Ask whether it truly does. Then see if you can turn it into emulation: wanting to rise to their level, not pull them down.
A119.example: Seeing a friend's book deal sting, then asking "what could I learn from how she worked?" turns the sting into a plan.

A120.plainWords: Emulation is distress at lacking something valued that others have, with a drive to get it. Unlike envy, it doesn't want to take it from them. It wants to rise. Turn envy into emulation.
A120.example: A junior designer who sees a colleague's polished portfolio and starts studying how it's built is emulating.

A121.plainWords: Persuasion rests on character, audience feeling, and the argument. Aristotle says character matters most. So build credibility through who you are, not through clever talk.
A121.example: A colleague with a record of being straight gets listened to even when her slides are plain.

A122.plainWords: Emotions shape what you see, what you notice, and what you conclude. The wise person doesn't suppress them. They understand what they're doing and use them as information.
A122.example: Feeling uneasy before signing a contract, and asking what that unease points to, is using the emotion as data.

K001.plainWords: Before you think "I am looking at a tree," there's just the looking. Nishida's point is that the split into me here and tree there comes second, after the experience. Labels are handy. They're also a layer on top, and a lot of our tiredness lives in that layer. Go back to the raw moment now and then.
K001.example: Hearing a song you love and, for ten seconds, nobody is listening and nothing is being listened to. Then you think "this is nice," and the moment has already changed.

K002.plainWords: Standing apart as an "I" looking at the world isn't where you start. You start inside the engagement and only later step back and build the observer. That reverses the usual burden of proof: the separate self is what needs explaining, and anything made can be looked at as made.
K002.example: In a crowded room you become aware of yourself as a watched object and suddenly can't walk normally. Thirty seconds earlier you were just walking.

K003.plainWords: Looking harder inward won't reveal the true self. Early Nishida says it shows up when you act with your whole attention, when knowing and willing are one. The carving into "a decider" and "a decision" comes afterwards. So trust wholehearted action as a source of self-knowledge, more than the inner commentary.
K003.example: A good cook mid-service doesn't feel like she is deciding anything. The self at that moment is more real than the one that evaluates dinner afterwards.

K004.plainWords: Every experience you have goes through one instrument, your mind, and an instrument that's never been checked distorts everything it measures. The Tibetan teachers turn this into a standing habit: look at the mind regularly, carefully, the way a mother watches her only child.
K004.example: Setting a timer at three in the afternoon and asking yourself, "What am I like right now?" Irritable. Hungry. Rehearsing an argument. Just knowing it changes the next hour.

K005.plainWords: Shantideva's bold claim is that fear and suffering arise from the mind. He isn't saying circumstances don't matter. He's saying the link between what happens and how much it hurts runs through your interpretation, and that is the part you can always reach.
K005.example: Two people get the same message, "we need to talk." One spends the day in dread. The other thinks it's probably logistics. The text is identical.

K006.plainWords: Speech, work, relationships: they're all downstream of the state of your mind, like a harvest from water. Guarding the mind isn't clamping down on it. It means watching it, so you know your states as they arise. That includes what you let in: the media, the company, the places.
K006.example: Noticing that every time you read certain news before bed you wake up irritable, and quietly stopping. Not suppressing anything, just choosing the water.

K007.plainWords: Thoughts, images and feelings appear. Awareness is the space they appear in. One is busy and gripping, the other quiet and always there. The Mahamudra teachers say nearly every practice is a way of shifting your weight from the first to the second.
K007.example: In a heated meeting, noticing that you're furious and noticing that there's a you who is noticing. The fury doesn't vanish, but it has stopped being the only thing in the room.

K008.plainWords: Nishitani says to expect a moment when the structure of meaning gives way, through grief, betrayal, illness, or just the slow erosion of what you used to believe. What opens is a sense that the ground is empty. Don't rush to patch it. It's a passage, and it may be the beginning of something.
K008.example: After a divorce, the career you built suddenly feels like a stage set. Nothing means what it did. Wise friends let you sit there before offering the next plan.

K009.plainWords: In Zen, great doubt isn't being unsure about lunch. It's a deep questioning of the self and everything you take for certain, kept alive until it swallows everything else. Doubt here is fuel, and comfortable certainty is what gets in the way.
K009.example: At forty, someone who has always known what they wanted asks, with no drama, "What if I never knew?" and doesn't hurry to answer.

K010.plainWords: When your ego's project falls apart, don't rebuild it in the same place. Step back to the ground that the ego grew out of. Nishitani says even the stepping back needs another step, since the stepper is still there. From there, things stop being supports or threats to your story and show up as what they are.
K010.example: After a public failure, you stop drafting your comeback story. For a day you just notice the weather, the dishes, a friend's voice, as they are.

K011.plainWords: The ego has no solid base. It borrows its shape from what it reflects, like a shadow. That isn't an insult, it's a fact with a consequence: you can't defend a fortress that isn't there, and all the energy spent defending it is spent on nothing.
K011.example: Someone corrects you in public and your whole body tightens. Asking "what exactly am I protecting?" makes the tightness a bit silly and a lot easier to drop.

K012.plainWords: Even insight into groundlessness can be turned into an identity: "I'm the one who sees through everything." That rebuilds the ego one floor down. The tradition says walk the passage, don't own it. The test is whether you can still be ordinary, patient and warm.
K012.example: The friend who has been to three retreats and now corrects everyone's attachments at dinner is wearing his awakening like a badge.

K013.plainWords: Some questions aren't gaps in information. They're instruments. "Who am I when no role is active?" does its work by being held open. Closing it early with a borrowed answer is, for this tradition, what an unexamined life is.
K013.example: Carrying "what is this before I name it?" around for a month, glancing at it while washing dishes, without trying to answer.

K014.plainWords: Absolute nothingness isn't an empty hole where things used to be. It's the place that lets things be things. The sky's emptiness is what makes clouds possible. When a structure in your life falls away, ask what can now appear that it was occupying.
K014.example: After losing a role at work, a person who has no title gradually finds time and attention for a friendship that had been squeezed out.

K015.plainWords: On the ground of emptiness, things return to themselves. The tree is a tree, the person in front of you is just that person, not a prop in your project. That "suchness" cures the habit of treating everything and everyone as a means. Try it once a day.
K015.example: Having lunch with a colleague and, for ten minutes, wanting nothing from them. They notice something is different, and so do you.

K016.plainWords: First you negate the self's claims: I'm not what I thought I was. Then you negate that, too: the emptiness I reached isn't a new place to stand. One negation yields nihilism or coolness. The second brings you back to ordinary life, now transparent. After letting go of an identity, finish by going back to your life.
K016.example: After deciding "I'm not my career," you don't become a drifter or a monk. You go back to work, a bit more lightly, and notice the colleague you used to overlook.

K017.plainWords: The Kyoto thinkers insist that nothingness isn't an exit from life. It's deeper engagement. The person on this ground works, loves and grieves without the extra weight of self-reference. The test isn't altered states but ordinary functioning. Judge any letting-go by whether your engagements get easier to be in.
K017.example: After a few weeks of practice, you're more available to your kids at dinner, not less. If you were drifting away from them, the practice was wrong, whatever it felt like.

K018.plainWords: Indra's net has a jewel at each knot, each reflecting all the others. Nothing is itself alone. Nishitani says things exist only in their mutual reference. Take that literally with the person you find hardest: they're not a separate unit to manage, they're a node in the same net you are.
K018.example: Before a tense conversation with your sister, you remind yourself that how she is with you is partly how you are with her, and your first sentence comes out softer.

K019.plainWords: Nishida's later logic says the real isn't uniform. One and many, self and world, individual and community are related as contradictory identity: each needs the other. That's not permission for sloppy thinking. It's noticing that the deepest things, a person, a marriage, a self, hold opposites together.
K019.example: In a good marriage, closeness and independence pull in opposite directions, and the couple that thrives learns to live inside the pull rather than pick a side.

K020.plainWords: Some knowledge only comes through doing. The potter knows the clay by working it, the surgeon the tissue by cutting, the parent the child by raising her. It doesn't arrive before action; action makes it. A culture that over-values preparation misses this.
K020.example: You can read about hospice care for a year and still know nothing until you sit with someone who is dying.

K021.plainWords: The body isn't a vehicle the self drives; it's the self's own way of being in the world. When you use a hammer well, you extend into it. The edge of your body is drawn by activity, not skin. Respect the tools and spaces that have become part of you.
K021.example: A pianist who loses her instrument after a house fire grieves like she's lost a limb. That's accurate, not dramatic.

K022.plainWords: Each person is a point where the world becomes aware of itself, a unique perspective the world sees through. That dignifies you without isolating you. You aren't a spectator of your era; you're one of its organs. Ask what your particular place, generation, wounds and gifts let you see that others can't.
K022.example: A nurse who grew up in poverty notices what the polished report misses about who can't afford the discharge plan.

K023.plainWords: The Kyoto School ends on purpose with something plain: after the collapse, the doubt and the stepping back, you return to dishes, work and family, minus the self-referential noise. The tradition's name for it is the ordinary mind, and its marks are patience, warmth and availability. Ordinariness is the measure.
K023.example: A person who has spent years on retreats and reading shows it by being the one who quietly stays to wash up.

K024.plainWords: Four thoughts turn the mind: this human life is rare and valuable; it ends; actions have consequences; drifting costs you. The instruction is to spend minutes, not hours, on them every day. Start by noticing what's working, what's finite, what you're doing, and what you're wasting.
K024.example: Thirty seconds at the kitchen table before the day starts: I'm healthy enough to be here, this won't last, what I do today matters, and I'm wasting an hour on my phone each night.

K025.plainWords: Treat experience as dream-like. That doesn't mean nothing is real. It means the mind's constructions, the interpretations, identities and grievances, have a dream's quality: vivid, gripping, and made. It's a standing habit of lightness toward your own certainties.
K025.example: Replaying an insult for the fifth time, you ask what it will weigh in a year, in five, at death. It deflates, a little.

K026.plainWords: The slogan says to rest in the nature of awareness itself, the plain knowing before any content. Lojong includes a wordless resting practice alongside the slogans, and the two feed each other. End a sitting with a minute of that, without doing anything.
K026.example: After twenty minutes working with slogans, you drop them for sixty seconds and just sit, aware, with nothing to fix.

K027.plainWords: After sitting, carry the dream-lightness into the day. A child of illusion engages fully without being taken in. A stage professional knows the set is a set and acts anyway, and acts better. Choose your most absorbing activity and practise doing it fully while knowing it's constructed.
K027.example: Giving a big presentation completely, and also quietly knowing it's one presentation among many, you speak with more freedom.

K028.plainWords: Tonglen means breathing in what hurts, yours or someone else's, and breathing out what helps. It's tied to the breath because the breath is always there and always has a rhythm, so you can do it in real situations. The direction is the training: it reverses the reflex to flee pain and cling to comfort.
K028.example: Sitting with a friend's grief in the hospital corridor and quietly breathing in her fear, breathing out something steady.

K029.plainWords: Three objects, three poisons, three seeds of virtue. Pleasing things trigger attachment, threatening ones aversion, neutral ones confusion. The practice is to catch the poison at the moment it fires and turn it into contentment, clarity or engaged compassion. Name today's poison as it happens.
K029.example: In a meeting you feel a flash of irritation at a colleague and say to yourself "aversion," and the clarity arrives half a second later.

K030.plainWords: Work with your strongest delusion first. Each person has a signature pattern, and it's running your life. Don't practise only on the comfortable edges. Ask three people who love you what yours is. The answer is usually common knowledge to everyone but you.
K030.example: Your sister says, "You always need to be right," your partner nods, and your closest friend laughs. That's your work.

K031.plainWords: Do the practice with no inner ledger expecting a return. Expectation turns practice into a transaction, and transactions collapse when the reward is late. This isn't against goals, it's against gripping them. Once a week, practise with the frame "this is not going anywhere."
K031.example: Sitting for ten minutes with no plan to become calmer, and noticing you're calmer than usual.

K032.plainWords: Whatever goes wrong, illness, insult, failure, fear, treat it as raw material rather than interruption. Mishap can't be prevented, so the only free variable is what you do with it. Make "what does this make possible?" your standing question about adversity.
K032.example: A cancelled flight becomes a day in a city you'd never have chosen, and a conversation that mattered.

K033.plainWords: Drive all blames into one. It sounds harsh and is precise: look at your own part first. This isn't self-blame, which is another fixation. It's engineering. Your own conduct is the part of the system you can reach. In any conflict, finish the sentence "my part in this was..." before the other's.
K033.example: After an argument with your manager, you write down your three contributions before drafting the email. It's a different email.

K034.plainWords: Be grateful to everyone. Even the difficult people are practice material, and gratitude keeps the heart from closing while you do the work. The ones who trigger you show you what's left to learn, which makes them teachers, unsentimentally. At day's end, include the hardest person on your list.
K034.example: Thanking, in your head, the colleague whose interruptions showed you how much you crave being heard.

K035.plainWords: Five strengths for the whole of life: strong determination, deciding once what the practice is; the white seed, accumulating the good day by day; reproach of the ego, meeting each flare of self-centredness with "there you are again"; aspiration, dedicating the fruits beyond yourself; steady familiarisation, the long boring middle.
K035.example: A dull Tuesday, no inspiration at all, and you sit anyway. That's the fifth strength doing its work.

K036.plainWords: Six warnings. Don't be patient with the wrong things, and impatient with what damages you. Don't aim at the wrong virtues, like calm in place of honesty. Don't confuse endurance with growth. Don't be predictable in your reactions. Don't be touchy about the conditions of practice. Mistaking the form for the substance is the usual trap.
K036.example: Someone proud of being calm in a toxic job isn't practising patience. They're avoiding a hard decision.

K037.plainWords: Harm comes from three places: people, events, and your own past actions catching up. Each needs a different first response: patience for people, problem-solving for events, ownership for consequences. Most conflict escalates because the responses are swapped.
K037.example: A leaking roof isn't someone's fault. Treating it as an insult wastes a week. Treating a colleague's rudeness as a plumbing problem fails too.

K038.plainWords: If there's a remedy, why be angry? If there's none, what use is anger? Suffering is either actionable or not, and anger belongs to neither: in the first case it wastes the energy the fix needs; in the second it adds a second pain to the first. At the next flare, ask just that.
K038.example: Stuck in traffic with nothing to do, anger only adds to the hour. Stuck in a billing dispute, anger loses you the call.

K039.plainWords: The enemy who injures you does something your friends can't: gives you the raw material of patience. Nobody else supplies it. That's not gratitude for harm. It's recognising the role difficult people play in your training that no one else applied for. Hold one difficult person in mind in that light.
K039.example: The relative who criticises you at every holiday is, by this view, your most reliable patience trainer.

K040.plainWords: Anger destroys what you're trying to protect. No evil compares to anger, no discipline to patience, and one flare can undo the merit of a thousand kindnesses, as one fire takes a forest. The argument isn't moral, it's prudential. Price the blast radius before letting anger run a situation.
K040.example: A single furious email to a client undoes two years of goodwill. The cost-benefit is lopsided.

K041.plainWords: Harm doesn't come from a free, unconditioned will that simply chose evil. It comes from conditions: a person's history, state, ignorance and situation, just as your own harms come from yours. That's dependent origination applied to forgiveness. Hatred aims at a villain, and the villain isn't quite there.
K041.example: A driver who cuts you off was perhaps up all night with a sick child. Not an excuse, but a different object for your anger.

K042.plainWords: The body is a vessel for doing good, to be maintained like any instrument. It's not a treasure to pamper or an enemy to punish. That framing cuts through two modern extremes: the body as display and the body as a machine to override. Look after it so it can carry you.
K042.example: Sleeping properly before a big week, not for vanity and not as a grudging chore, just because the vessel has work to do.

K043.plainWords: The method of vigilance is to keep coming back to the state of your mind, moment by moment, tenderly, like a mother watching her only child. The difference between that and surveillance is warmth. Surveillance is anxious. Care is kind about what it sees.
K043.example: Noticing you're tense in the afternoon and saying "ah, tense," as you would to a child who's tired, without a verdict.

K044.plainWords: Make speech relevant, gentle and well timed, and train in the pause between having something to say and saying it. Speech is the mind's most irreversible output, and most regret is shaped like a sentence. In your next charged conversation add two breaths.
K044.example: Someone says something unfair in a meeting. You wait two breaths, and what comes out is a question rather than a verdict.

K045.plainWords: The reflex that always puts your own welfare first is the root of most chronic trouble with relationships and meaning. Self-care isn't wrong. The priority is a quirk of perspective: from the whole, you are one case among billions, and your suffering is one among many.
K045.example: In a queue, someone rushes ahead and you boil. Later you realise the whole day was organised around "me first," including your irritation.

K046.plainWords: Run a thought-exercise until it reshapes your instincts: stand in the other person's place and view your conduct from there. Regard your own body, possessions and status as available to others' needs, the way theirs are to you, and practise the reversal. The change comes by repeating it, not by agreeing with it.
K046.example: Before a tense phone call, imagine being the person on the other end hearing your tone. Then make the call.

K047.plainWords: All the happiness in the world, says the chapter, comes from wishing others well, and all the suffering from wishing only yourself well. It's bold and testable in small. Look back over a week and mark the hours that mattered most. Most were probably spent in service, love, teaching or making.
K047.example: A person looks back on their calendar and finds the best moments were helping a neighbour move and cooking for a friend, not the promotion.

K048.plainWords: In disputes, let the other person be right, or at least heard, and give credit for joint work to others deliberately, as training, not as loss. The reasoning isn't saintly. The credit-hoarding self is a heavy thing to carry, and most of its weight is upkeep.
K048.example: After a successful project, you name your colleague's contribution in the meeting before she has to, and feel lighter on the walk home.

K049.plainWords: The lamrim is a graduated path in which each reflection motivates the next: this life's value and ending, the effects of action, the wish for a steady mind, then equanimity, gratitude and the vast motivation. Skipping steps produces advanced practices on unprepared foundations, with predictable results.
K049.example: Someone attempts to practise radical compassion without ever having dealt with their own resentment, and it curdles into performance.

K050.plainWords: The capacities you have now, health, freedom, literacy, time, are rare across human history. The reflection turns them from background assumptions into fuel. It's paired with impermanence so urgency doesn't turn into anxiety. The point is to use them, not to panic.
K050.example: Reading a book on a quiet afternoon and remembering that for most people in history that would have been impossible. You read it differently.

K051.plainWords: Every action leaves a disposition, and dispositions shape what's easy to do next. Set aside rebirth and what remains is habit, exactly. Treat each repetition of a pattern as a vote for the person you're becoming.
K051.example: Each night you snap at the kids "just this once," and by the end of the month it's who you are at 6pm.

K052.plainWords: Start by levelling the mind's bias toward friends, enemies and strangers, so later practices of gratitude, love and compassion stand on level ground rather than preference. The tradition's image is that every being has, across time, been everything to you, kind and unkind.
K052.example: Waiting at a bus stop, you wish the stranger beside you, the one who irritates you, the same ease you'd wish a friend.

K053.plainWords: Everything you can do was given: language, food, roads, the people who raised you. The tradition trains a deliberate meditation on that, as an accurate correction to the mind's default belief that you made yourself. Once a week, trace one capability back through the hands that gave it.
K053.example: Tracing how you came to cook: your grandmother, the market vendor, the farmer, the person who wrote the recipe.

K054.plainWords: Bodhicitta means intending that your own growth in wisdom and ability serve everyone, and holding it as the frame of ordinary life rather than a separate project. Whatever you're getting good at, name who it serves, and let the naming widen.
K054.example: Learning to code, you add "so I can build tools that help people in my town" and notice your motivation on hard days changes.

K055.plainWords: Generosity is the first perfection, and the instruction is graded. Start with small, real gifts of time, attention, money in amounts that stretch you a little, because the practice is loosening the grip, and the grip loosens through repetition. The measure is the inner event, not the size of the gift.
K055.example: Giving up an evening to help a friend move, when you'd rather rest, and noticing a small release.

K056.plainWords: Start the perfection of ethics at the floor: not killing, stealing, lying, dividing people or speaking cruelly. A mind at war with its own conduct can't settle. Keep the floor unconditionally for one season before aspiring to the ceiling.
K056.example: For three months you tell no lies, not even white ones, and notice how quiet your head becomes.

K057.plainWords: The remaining perfections come in order: patience, energy, concentration, wisdom. Energy is the aliveness of effort, trained against both laziness and burnout. Concentration is the ability to rest and bind attention. Wisdom is the seeing-through. Each one is a perfection when it's pursued for the sake of others.
K057.example: A teacher trains patience with a struggling student, then energy to keep trying new approaches, then focus to read what is actually going on, then the wisdom to know when to stop.

K058.plainWords: Saraha's instruction is to leave the mind unaltered: don't modify it, don't manufacture a meditative state, don't reject what arises. It sounds like "do nothing." The tradition says it's an active skill: it takes precision not to add the usual interference.
K058.example: Sitting down and, instead of trying to calm yourself, letting restlessness be restlessness, and finding it settles on its own after a while.

K059.plainWords: Thoughts aren't the enemy of meditation. They're the mind's own movement, as waves are the sea's. Let each one arise, be seen and dissolve without following or fighting it. You don't have to still the sea to know the water. In sitting, count the gap between waves.
K059.example: A thought about tomorrow's meeting arises, you notice it, and it fades before you've followed it anywhere.

K060.plainWords: Tilopa's six words: don't recall, don't imagine, don't think, don't examine, don't control, rest. The first five are the mind's ways of leaving the present: retrieving, projecting, narrating, analysing, managing. The sixth is what's left when they stop. Use them as a portable reset.
K060.example: Standing in a queue with a racing mind, you run through the six words and arrive, for a moment, in the queue.

K061.plainWords: There are two ways to work with thoughts: what they say, or what they are. Working on content never ends, because content is inexhaustible. Seeing a thought as an event in awareness is direct. When a thought loop won't yield to analysis, switch modes and examine the thinking itself.
K061.example: Stuck in "what if I fail," you stop arguing with the thought and just see: a thought, a tightening in the chest, a thought.

K062.plainWords: One taste means that someone who has seen the nature of mind tastes the same in meditation and out of it, in pleasant and unpleasant, in sacred and ordinary. The differences remain; the underlying field doesn't change. The test is transfer: what you can reach on the cushion should be there in traffic.
K062.example: The calm you find on the cushion holds, a little, when your phone rings at an awkward moment.

K063.plainWords: Milarepa's songs keep warning that the spectacular, visions, powers, ecstasies, is practice's decoration and its trap. The plain person who has dropped grandiosity does better than the visionary who has acquired it. When something impressive happens, tell one grounded friend and then forget it.
K063.example: After a striking experience on retreat you mention it to your sister, and she says "that's nice, did you call mum?" and it's just right.

K064.plainWords: Milarepa advises householders: the austere life is support, not the point. For you it means simplicity and clean conduct, not mountain asceticism. Practice stands on honest livelihood, simple needs, and conduct you wouldn't need to hide.
K064.example: A parent with a job, a mortgage and a sick relative practises by working honestly, keeping needs modest, and not lying at the school gate.

K065.plainWords: Tanabe says reason's project of grounding itself fails at its own edge, and there what the thinker needs isn't a better argument but metanoia: a turning of the whole mind, closer to repentance than proof. In practice, when you've honestly exhausted your own resources, stop arguing harder and confess you can't.
K065.example: After months of trying to fix a relationship with logic, you finally say "I don't know what to do," and for the first time it moves.

K066.plainWords: In psychological terms, Tanabe's death and resurrection means letting the self that planned and controlled fail, and what acts afterwards isn't a new ego claiming victory but a self that knows it is carried by factors it didn't create. That's his "other-power," borrowed from Pure Land and stated philosophically.
K066.example: After a long illness you stop managing recovery and let others help, and find that you are held more than you thought.

K067.plainWords: Tanabe's logic of the species says you don't exist first and then join groups. You're formed in and through family, nation, craft. The self that ignores that is an abstraction. So serving your community isn't giving yourself up. It's part of how you became yourself.
K067.example: A craftsperson realises her skill is a gift from her teachers and community, and teaching an apprentice feels less like sacrifice and more like repayment.

K068.plainWords: Tanabe's metanoetics ends in thankfulness. The self that couldn't ground itself finds it was already held, and the fitting response is a life of gratitude, not a doctrine. It's trained like any stance, by repetition in small matters. End each day by naming one thing that was given.
K068.example: Before sleep, you think: the neighbour who watered the plants, the bus driver's nod, the tea. Not earned, just given.

K069.plainWords: Hisamatsu's name for what these practices converge on is a self without fixed form: it doesn't identify with its contents. His test questions are ordinary and brutal. What is your fundamental perspective? If every role and achievement were removed, what remains? The formless self isn't a blank. It's what has no fixed shape.
K069.example: A retired surgeon, with no title and no patients, finds that she's still curious, still kind, and still herself.

K070.plainWords: Hisamatsu's compass has three parts: awaken the formless self; take all humankind as your horizon, not your tribe; act from beyond your historical moment's assumptions. They're one discipline of perspective, usable on a Tuesday. When a conflict or decision arrives, run through all three.
K070.example: Facing a workplace dispute, you ask: what am I clinging to, how would this look to everyone affected, and what would someone a century from now notice?

K071.plainWords: The last of the ox-herding pictures shows the sage returning to the marketplace with open hands: no teachings, just available. It's this book's final principle because everything pointed here: the collapse, the nothingness, the mind work, all of it ends up as being useful and plain in ordinary life.
K071.example: After years of practice, someone is simply the person who always has time for the neighbour's problem.

PP001.plainWords: There are two broad ways of doing well. One is feeling good: pleasure, satisfaction, few bad moods. The other is a life with meaning, purpose and growth. They overlap, but they're not the same, and a life can be full of the first and thin on the second.
PP001.example: A well-paid job with great holidays can be pleasant for years, and still leave you wondering what any of it is for.

PP002.plainWords: A third kind of good life has been proposed: the psychologically rich one, interesting and varied, full of experiences that change how you see things. You can be comfortable and meaningful and still not particularly interesting. Richness values novelty and perspective.
PP002.example: Spending six months in a country where you don't speak the language may not be pleasant or purposeful, but it leaves you seeing everything differently.

PP003.plainWords: Well-being is hard to measure. Self-report depends on your mood that day, on cultural habits of answering, and on wanting to look good. Body measures like heart-rate variability add something but miss the felt side. Treat any single number with suspicion.
PP003.example: Asked "how satisfied are you with your life?" on a sunny Friday, you'd give a higher number than on a rainy Monday.

PP004.plainWords: Flourishing isn't one variable. PERMA names five parts: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment. Other models add health, money and stability. No single dimension is enough, and someone high in achievement but low in relationships isn't flourishing.
PP004.example: A successful surgeon with no close friends and a good salary would score high on one side and low on another.

PP005.plainWords: Positive feeling is part of well-being, not all of it. Someone happy because they're drunk or cut off from reality isn't flourishing. The measure is the pattern of a life: functioning well, feeling well, and being well in the world.
PP005.example: A person euphoric from a manic episode feels great while their life is quietly falling apart.

PP006.plainWords: Autonomy is feeling that your actions are your own, in line with your values and interests, not driven by outside pressure or inner compulsion. It isn't independence. It predicts engagement and persistence.
PP006.example: Going for a run because you want to feels different from going because a tracker nags you.
